name: ptx-gpu-sim
targets: GPU performance analysis and profiling metrics
bullets: Built a cycle-level SIMT GPU simulator in C++17 that runs CUDA PTX, modeling warp schedulers, IPDOM branch divergence, memory coalescing, shared-memory bank conflicts and L1/L2/DRAM
Wrote 14 CUDA/PTX kernels (SGEMM, transpose, reductions, histogram); simulator showed tiling cuts SGEMM global loads 16x and 32x33 padding removes transpose bank conflicts (1.55x)
Validated with 60 tests and GitHub Actions CI that assembles PTX with ptxas and runs nvcc-generated PTX; warp-shuffle reduction measured 1.56x faster than divergent version

summary.what: A C++17 cycle-level SIMT GPU simulator that executes PTX kernels (hand-written or produced by nvcc from CUDA C++) and reports the hardware metrics that explain kernel performance: IPC, SIMD efficiency, sectors per request, bank-conflict wavefronts, cache hit rates, occupancy and per-scheduler stall reasons.
summary.how: A PTX parser feeds a CFG/post-dominator pass that gives every branch its reconvergence point; an engine dispatches CTAs to SMs under warp/register/shared-memory limits, issues one instruction per scheduler per cycle (GTO or round-robin) with a register scoreboard, executes all 32 lanes functionally, and times memory through a sector coalescer, 32-bank shared-memory model, sectored L1/L2 caches and bandwidth-limited DRAM. Results are checked against CPU references; CI validates the PTX with ptxas and runs nvcc's PTX for the same kernels.
summary.hardest: Getting divergence and timing right together: computing immediate post-dominators so the per-warp SIMT stack reconverges at the right pc (including early returns and loops with per-lane trip counts), and fast-forwarding idle cycles while still charging every scheduler cycle to exactly one stall reason, which a test checks sums to cycles x SMs x schedulers.
summary.say: I built a GPU simulator that runs real PTX, including what nvcc emits, and models warps, divergence, coalescing, bank conflicts, caches and occupancy. It let me measure why optimizations work, for example padding a transpose tile to 33 columns drops shared-memory wavefronts per request from 16.5 to 1. The numbers are from an uncalibrated model, so I use it to explain kernel variants, not to predict real GPU timings.
